In 1792, when estahhshing the Post Office, Congress set the 
postage rates, and it decreed fists of towns through which the post 
roads had to pass, but it empowered the Postmaster General to 
prescribe such regulations” to all persons “employed under , as 
may be found necessary, and to superintend the business of the 
department.” This rulemaking and superintending power covered 
major decisions over which the Postmaster General had broad 
discretion: to designate roads beyond those specified by statute, with 
no express criteria; to decide the location of ah post offices wherever 
‘‘such shall be found necessary”; and to provide for the delivery of mail 
“as often as he .. . shall think proper,” the only standard being to 
have “regard to the productiveness” of the mail, “as well as other 
circumstances,” which meant a lot of discretion considering that^the 
post office could use all the money it made and remained in the black 
for forty years. * * *
In 1794, Congress authorized the President “whenever, in his 
opinion, the public safety shall so require, to lay an embargo on all 
ships and vessels in the ports of the United States, or upon the ships 
and vessels of the United States, or the ships and vessels of any 
foreign nation, under such regulations as the circumstances of the 
case may require, and to continue or revoke the same, whenever he 
shall think proper,” provided that such embargo started while 
Congress was out of session and expired within fifteen days of the 
start of the upcoming session, which meant a window from June 
through November that year. * * *
In 1798, Congress imposed a tax on commercial seamen’s wages 
and told the President, using the sums collected in each port, to 
“provide for the temporary rehef and maintenance of sick or disabled 
seamen [in that port], in the hospitals or other proper institutions 
now estabhshed” there, “or in ports where no such institutions exist, 
then in such other manner as he shall direct,” and ultimately to build 
seamen’s hospitals in the ports. The act also provided for marine-
hospital “directors” in each port “to provide for the accommodation of 
sick and disabled seamen, under such general instructions as shall 
be given by the President of the United States, for that purpose, and 
also subject to the like general instructions, to direct and govern such 
hospitals” as might be built. The act provided no criteria regarding 
which seamen were ehgible for rehef, or for what types of care or 
benefits, and the “general instructions” were in fact employed to 
impose controversial pohcies about ehgibihty in subsequent years.
